title: Godot or Unity for AI-assisted development?
author: Afterlight_Games
selftext:
I use Claude pretty heavily in my development, and I'm wondering what everyone else here is using

From what I understand, AI tends to work better with Godot since its scene files are plain text it can read and edit directly, but Unity has the bigger asset store and community

Which engine are you on (Godot, Unity, something else) and which AI? Has one worked noticeably better for you?

comments.author: zenmatrix83
comments.body: Your end goal matters, they are both good options, unreal as well

replies.author: megaflutter
replies.body: People are saying don’t do unreal but the graphics are so, so good. I think once you have a good direction of your gameplay mechanics, moving to unreal engine is worth it. Also makes your game look less like AI slop.

replies.author: zenmatrix83
replies.body: Unity and godot are great, but for a serious 3d game unreal is best, it’s just harder I think to use

replies.author: megaflutter
replies.body:
It’s just that Unreal is a token hog. They need to optimize their MCP for better token/output value.

Once you get the foundation set up though, you can start flying.

comments.body:
Three.js gets a prototype in minutes, but a while to look half-decent. 
Unity/unreal gets you AAA walking simulator out of the box in seconds, but takes a while to actually build anything in. 


The best approach for me is to build the whole thing in three.js with placeholders and then have an agent rewrite the whole thing in either unity or unreal with better models and graphics.

replies.author: Level3Super
replies.body: Please explain the placeholder and how you get the agent to write in another engine. Thanks

Placeholders = some free assets that are fully rigged. Enough to unblock end-to-end development but not enough for a fully finished/polished game. 

Think random low-poly model with 150+ animations for everything you may ever want. Just change the color of their hat, and make it indicative of what sort of character it is. 

Once everything is fully written, and works end to end, decide on which engine you want to use for game polish. Agents will be able to work on ALL assets in parallel, and convert your entire game in a fraction of the time it would have taken them to develop it from scratch. Just tell them which engine to convert the whole game into and let them handle it.

replies.author: megaflutter
replies.body: I have a similar workflow and noticed the same when changing engines. It’s faster once you have the mechanics nailed down.

replies.author: megaflutter
replies.body: I always start with “begin with low poly boxes“ so that I can validate the gameplay mechanics first. This gets you to faster a prototype.

comments.author: Weaves87
comments.body:
I've been using Godot w/ the Godot MCP Toolkit (the one in the Godot Asset Store - there are several MCPs for Godot but this is the best one imo). I have been quite impressed with it so far, at least for a 2D game.

Most Godot files are text based, which obviously Claude can work with well on its own, but the MCP toolkit allows it to launch the game and send inputs, capture screenshots, and do all kinds of ingame debugging/telemetry capture, etc. Basically makes it so that most anything you can do in the editor it can do as well.

I like this setup a lot because I have Godot running on my Windows machine, but Claude Code running in a Linux VM (windows linux subsystem) and talking to the MCP that is running in Windows. This isolates Claude so it can't really poke around on the Windows machine and touch anything its not supposed to, and can only work on the Godot project

comments.body: Godot is lighter and faster. I prefer it for many reasons, but you should not discount the fact that Unity has shitty business practices and Godot is free and open source.
